metadata.note: Dr. William Seward Webb -- president of the Wagner Palace Car Company and a Vanderbilt in-law -- pushed a railroad straight through the roadless middle of the Adirondacks in 1891-92, the last great piece of New York State to get one. He began by buying the narrow-gauge Herkimer, Newport & Poland (built 1882, 16 miles) and regauging it, then built north from Remsen through Thendara, Big Moose and Tupper Lake to Malone, opening in the fall of 1892 with through trains from Herkimer all the way to Montreal. The New York Central took the line over in May 1893, moved the southern terminus from Herkimer to Utica, and in 1913 absorbed it outright as the Adirondack Division. It was never a money-maker: it existed to carry sportsmen, tuberculosis patients bound for Saranac Lake, and the private cars of the Adirondack great camps. Service north of Malone toward Montreal ended in 1953, the main line was cut back from Malone to Lake Clear Junction in 1957, and the last New York Central passenger train ran Apr 24 1965. Penn Central abandoned freight north of Remsen in 1972, New York State bought the whole Utica-Lake Placid corridor in 1974 for the 1980 Winter Olympics, and after an Adirondack Railway revival in 1979-81 the corridor is now a tourist railroad (Utica-Tupper Lake) and, north of Tupper Lake, a rail trail.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: Timetable frequencies for any era -- all headways here are estimates. Also unsourced: the exact abandonment dates of the Lake Clear Junction-Malone line and of the Herkimer-Poland-Remsen branch, and the dates each intermediate station closed. Also unsourced: the date the Saranac Lake - Lake Placid track was lifted for the Adirondack Rail Trail (October 2020 and 2022 are both reported, and the conflict is left unresolved), and whether any scheduled train used the Lake Clear Junction - Saranac Lake branch between 1981 and its conversion to trail.
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API), ways tagged railway=rail/abandoned/disused/razed/dismantled, routed between the station waypoints listed above with a shortest-path search over the OSM rail graph. metadata.freight_only_audit: 2026-08-24: removed as part of a repo-wide freight-only audit. Removed here: segment 1965-1972 from nyc-adirondack-division-utica-lake-placid (explicitly 'Freight only' under NYC then Penn Central). REPO RULE: this map shows PASSENGER rail only. Freight-only operation is not represented -- a line's segments must end when its passenger service ends. See CONVENTIONS.md.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.ownership_split: 2026-08-24: the single Utica-Lake Placid feature was split into three at Lake Clear Junction and Saranac Lake, per CLAUDE.md Rule 4. It had drawn New York Central colour over the Saranac Lake - Lake Placid ten miles from 1892, but that track was the Delaware and Hudson's Saranac and Lake Placid line until the ICC approved its sale to the NYC on November 1, 1946 - the NYC reached Lake Placid on trackage rights before then, and the D&H era is already drawn in dh_chateaugay_lake_placid.geojson. The Lake Clear Junction - Saranac Lake portion is now its own feature, the Mohawk and Malone's 6.5-mile Saranac Branch of July 16, 1892.
metadata.nyc_company_split: 2026-08-24: compound "predecessor / New York Central Railroad" company strings split per CLAUDE.md Rule 4. The legend groups on the exact company string (app.js railroadsInView), so a compound string drew as a separate railroad from the New York Central even for years the NYC itself ran the trains. Each feature is now split at the date its own segment note names the new operator, into features with identical geometry: the predecessor keeps its name and colour for the earlier years, and the NYC-operated years become "New York Central Railroad" at #5C677D. The Pittsburgh and Lake Erie and the Big Four were renamed but NOT split -- both were NYC-controlled yet stayed separately operated railroads under their own names, so they keep their own legend row.
